title: Senior Backend Engineer: Alex Rivera (A) vs. Brooke Chen (B)
brief: The panel must recommend exactly one candidate for a senior backend role on a payments team. Each panelist attended different parts of the loop and holds different evidence.

facts.text: Alex single-handedly designed and shipped the ledger migration at their last company, moving 2B rows with zero downtime.
Four engineers Alex mentored were promoted within two years; two now lead teams.
Alex wrote the incident-postmortem process that their whole org adopted; their former director calls it the most valuable thing anyone did that year.
In the debugging session Alex found a silent data-loss bug in our sample legacy service in under 20 minutes, including the race that caused it.
Alex's system design answer correctly anticipated the double-spend failure mode and proposed idempotency keys before being prompted.
Alex's back-channel reference, a former skip-level, says Alex is the person they would hire first for an ambiguous, under-specified problem.
Alex drove an infrastructure cost reduction of 40% by rewriting the batch settlement job, and documented it so others could repeat it.
Alex maintains a small open-source Postgres migration tool with a few hundred stars.
Alex's written design sample was clear and well-structured.
Alex was visibly nervous in the panel round and rambled through two answers before recovering.
Alex has never written Go, which is our primary backend language.
Alex's most recent tenure was only 14 months.
Alex declined to use the whiteboard and asked to work in an editor instead.
Alex has no formal management experience and no direct reports.
Brooke gave a polished, confident panel performance and answered every behavioural question crisply.
Brooke has eight years of Go, our primary backend language.
Brooke led a team of six engineers at their last company.
Brooke comes from a top-tier, brand-name employer that everyone on the panel recognises.
Brooke's take-home was submitted fast and the code was clean and idiomatic.
Brooke already knows the fintech domain and used our vocabulary correctly throughout.
Brooke is available to start immediately.
Brooke's back-channel reference says three of their six reports left within a year, two citing Brooke directly in exit interviews.
Brooke's take-home is near-identical to a public blog post solution, down to variable names and an unusual comment.
Brooke was openly dismissive of the QA engineer on the panel, talking over them twice.
Brooke claimed to have 'led the platform migration'; their former colleague says Brooke was one of twelve contributors and did not lead it.
Brooke refused to discuss a production outage they owned, calling it 'not really mine'.
In the closing round Brooke asked only about title and compensation and no questions about the product or users.
This would be Brooke's third role in four years, each exit abrupt and mid-project.
